What hit me most about Obsession is that a day later, I still cannot stop thinking about it. And I think that’s because the film is operating on a much smarter level than its premise initially suggests. This is the kind of setup that could have gone wrong in so many obvious ways. It could have become broad “hashtag cinema,” where the creepy possessive guy simply learns a lesson about toxic masculinity. It also could have accidentally drifted into ugly territory where the film frames the woman as somehow deserving punishment for “friend-zoning” him, as if she had been manipulating his feelings all along. But what’s fascinating is that the movie avoids both traps almost entirely.

This film works because of how emotionally complicated the relationships actually are. When he makes the wish, the realization slowly creeps in that he probably never needed to make it in the first place. The film subtly suggests that there may have already been a real path toward intimacy between them if he had simply been direct, vulnerable, and emotionally honest. Instead, what he wants is a shortcut. That’s what the wish really represents. It’s not the creation of love, but the desire to bypass the difficult, awkward, human process of earning closeness naturally.

That idea feels deeply connected to modern dating culture. So much of contemporary romance now revolves around avoiding vulnerability altogether. Instead of slowly getting to know someone, people jump immediately toward manipulation, performance, sexual escalation, or emotional pressure. The film understands that impulse in a way that feels painfully current. He doesn’t use the wish because he has no path toward connection. He uses it because he is unwilling to risk the uncertainty and discomfort that real connection requires.

What makes this even more interesting is that their friendship before everything collapses is actually good. There is real affection between them. The movie never portrays her as somebody cynically keeping him around for validation while waiting for a “better” guy. Their relationship has warmth, humor, and genuine intimacy already built into it. Which is why the horror of the film becomes larger than simply “obsession.” The tragedy is that he destroys something meaningful because he cannot accept allowing it to evolve naturally.

And that’s why the film has just dug into my mind and won't let go. Underneath all the supernatural insanity, the film is really about what happens when people try to force relationships into forms they were never meant to take. Once coercion enters the equation, even subtly, people stop becoming authentic versions of themselves. The relationship itself becomes poisoned. The film understands that emotional manipulation exists far beyond magic wishes or horror-movie extremes. There are countless real-world ways people pressure, corner, guilt, or psychologically steer relationships into existence, and the movie taps into that discomfort without ever reducing itself to a simple moral lecture.

This is why Obsession feels more mature than it has any right to. It understands something many films ignore: sometimes a truly meaningful friendship is already a profound form of love. And sometimes the inability to recognize that can destroy the very thing you were trying to hold onto in the first place.

One of our clear favorites of the year, and without a doubt one of the strongest modern horror entries in recent memory. The one and only Curry Barker is genuinely on the verge of becoming one of the most exciting new voices in the genre, and after this excellent debut feature, it feels impossible to doubt that. Alongside Inde Navarrette, the two create something that feels disturbing, emotionally grounded, and unforgettable all at once.

Barker’s direction is nothing short of masterful, using lingering shots, oppressive shadows, and phenomenal sound design to amplify the sense of dread in every scene. Even in complete silence, the tension is executed so flawlessly, that the imagery alone is able to carry the horror effortlessly. What makes the film so effective is how grounded it feels despite its supernatural elements, constantly blurring the line between emotional reality and psychological nightmare.

At the center of it all is Navarrette, delivering an absolutely powerhouse performance. Her range of facial expressions is mesmerizing, and under Barker’s meticulous direction, she gradually transforms into something completely unrecognizable from the person she initially appears to be. From her physicality to the sudden shifts in emotion and personality, every movement feels unpredictable and deeply unsettling. Her erratic body language and haunting presence had specially Marina’s heart racing nonstop, and the performance genuinely leaves you disturbed long after the credits roll.

While Navarrette is undeniably the star of the film, the surrounding cast deserves immense credit for grounding the narrative in reality. Their relatable vulnerability and sense of normalcy provide the perfect contrast to her spiraling madness, making her transformation feel even more intense and horrifying.

Even with a relatively simple premise, the themes, commentary, and details woven throughout make the film far more compelling than it initially appears. Masterfully balancing different horrors (psychological, supernatural, body horror) and dark comedy without ever losing control of its tone. The tension escalates with every set piece, while the lighting, shadow work, and imagery create scenes that stay burned into your mind long after the film ends.

What makes it especially fascinating is how it explores some of the ugliest corners of modern love and relationship, such as the loss of female autonomy, the performative nature of “nice guys,” the emotional decay caused by co-dependency, and the way your deepest desires can slowly become your own prison. Beyond the increasingly sinister dynamic between Bear and Nikki, the story also paints this entire friend group as emotionally damaged people incapable of honest communication, turning the horror itself into the consequence of their own behavior.

There’s still so much left to unpack here, but this is the kind of film that deserves to be experienced with as little knowledge as possible. Personally, we found it gripping from beginning to end, and it delivers exactly what we want from horror cinema today, so we completely recommended. GIVE US MORE.

Ever see The Twilight Zone episode called “The Chaser”? It’s the one where a lovestruck man buys a love potion for $1, it works but the girl drives him nuts and the only way out is to buy the "glove cleaner" (poison) for $1,000, his entire savings. Throw a monkey’s paw into the mix and dial it up to ten. Welcome to Obsession.

I’ve seen all of Curry Barker’s short films and have recommended them all here on Letterboxd. Obsession is his highly anticipated first feature length film. Like the short films, you can tell the guy very much understands horror and how to present it in new and terrifying ways. For a relative newbie, he’s got a great eye, too. The camera often hides something ghastly but eventually reveals its dark-natured subject. I love it.

This production shows how dynamic Barker’s directorial chops are. His short films are incredibly efficient, packing so much character and atmosphere into a tiny space. Here we see the exact opposite. Obsession takes its sweet time, slowly unfolding, scene by scene. And each scene feels drawn out too, adding tension, one granule at a time. We’re just hanging there, waiting for it to explode.

Welcome to the big leagues, Curry Barker. You may be the horror genre’s rookie of the year.

A man’s complete blind spot to a woman’s personhood and interiority taken to cruel extremes — fun to pair with The Drama. Rewatching this movie, I think I found the kernel that separates it from its YouTube-to-cinema contemporaries: Rather than perpetuating shallow “isn’t it all so fucked up” provocations, Obsession sinks its audience into a gnawing discomfort. There’s a tightrope here that Curry Barker walks, and he wobbles to either get a laugh or a wince, but he never lets you forget that everything Bear does is violatingly evil. Obviously everyone is giving Inde Navarrette her due flowers for all the unbelievable gags, but the scenes where Nikki’s agency peeks through are some of the most upsetting things you’ll see all year.

What the film has going for it is Inde Navarrette’s performance. It is bold, inventive, biting, and revelatory in all the ways the film itself can only dream of embodying. As the film lurches to its obvious, mean-spirited conclusion, it is evident Nikki is merely a vehicle for shocking moments of brutal violence, gross-out dark humor, and male fears of women who are just too much. But Navarrette gives a stunning performance that clearly delineates between real-Nikki’s fear and whatever entity is housed in her body’s malevolent manic pixie nightmare act. She brings such remarkable detail to a character that is ultimately merely a tool for the film’s middling scares and lack of imagination. It isn’t a bad movie overall, I was entertained. But mostly I was frustrated.

There’s a damning scene that touches on the wounds Barker lacks the curiosity and ingenuity to explore. It comes late in the film, so this is spoiler territory....

Bear gets urgent texts from Sarah, another coworker who actually has a crush on him and has been worried, to meet immediately. He slips from the bed in order not to wake Nikki, when another moment in which the real Nikki breaks through occurs. While her body is sleeping, she speaks directly to him. “Bear, please kill me,” she repeatedly pleads. She mentions that “she”, as in the entity housed in Nikki’s body, is asleep. She begs to be freed from this hellish prison in which she is conscious of the horror happening but has no autonomy. She is forced to be a silent, unwilling witness to her own life’s degradation. “Is it so bad being with me?” Bear asks. “I’ve never been with you, Bear,” Nikki responds. As she continues to beg to be killed, Bear slinks deeper into the murky shadows of the room before leaving Nikki.

This is a moment of remarkable cowardice. I am not just talking about Bear’s refusal to look at the horror his actions have engendered. Whatever he feels for her is not love or care or even curiosity. He doesn’t even seem to care that who he has been with is not even the woman he said he loved. What I am actually talking about is the cowardice of the filmmaker himself.

This exchange between Nikki and Bear cements what was evident to me earlier in the film: every time these characters have had sex Nikki is essentially being raped. Even as it becomes undeniable to Bear that who he is engaging with isn’t actually Nikki — given the moments of fear that arise when her true self push through to the surface and the concerns from friends who don’t know what’s going on but feel Bear is taking advantage of her — he stays committed to the “relationship”. What makes Obsession interesting at all is in Nikki’s story. The idea of your control over your own body and your life being taken from you by a man you thought was your friend is genuinely terrifying. I couldn’t stop thinking of the fear and terror that would consume anyone’s psyche as they were present in a body they could no longer control, forced to witness repeated sexual encounters you didn’t consent to and the killing of those you love by your own hand. Instead, Barker shapes this premise into a tragedy about Bear’s self-inflicted journey. The movie is so eager to frame him as a victim, it loses out on a far richer line of inquiry and muddles its own story. The more I think about the film, the more damning its approach becomes. Yeah this was worth the hype. I wasn’t prepared for the sheer bleakness I just witnessed. The film starts off as your usual horror but once that switch happens everything changed.

At first it was hilarious, I could find humor at the bizarre moments. Absolutely awkward and tense but as a film I could have fun with it. But as the story progressed and stuff got way out of control it becomes utterly terrifying and painful. I didn’t know what to feel once the credits started rolling.

It has all the ingredients a horror film needs, creepy atmosphere, insanely tense moments, phenomenal performances, slick direction and a smart idea for a horror flick, but this one didn’t rely on ghosts to evoke fear, it just takes the seriousness of that smart idea to it’s fullest extent and that made for a dreadfully horrifying experience.

I don’t know what to feel about the outcome of the principal characters, it messed me up. It’s been a long time since a film made me feel this upset. One fact that still annoys me in these horror films is that it uses certain cliche plot devices to move the story forward. Here, if a person could just say what they want or listen to another person’s problems seriously or do something immediately when you realize things seem off, a whole lot of problems could have been avoided, but if the writing did that we wouldn’t have a movie. I wish in future these talented writers figure out a way to avoid falling into these annoying tropes to move the story forward. That’s the one issue I had with this film. I can’t dwell into this issue more without talking about spoilers.

Curry Barker blew me away. His writing was great but his direction was fantastic. Can’t wait to see what he comes up with in the future. Michael Johnston was brilliant, loved what he did with his character. But yeah, without a doubt Inde Navarrette stole the show with her exceptional performance. It’s easy to act crazy, I wasn’t blow away by that(she was great going crazy too) but she blew away in her disturbed emotional moments too. The voice breaking, the eyes bursting with tears and horror or her freaky smile, everything works. One of the best performances I’ve seen in a horror film.

But yeah at the end, it’s the tragic nature of the story that stays with you. That naive feeling of “what could have happened if he/she did that instead of this” haunted me.I’m wrecked, this one really got me. I’m gonna just leave it at that.

Rewatched Obsession to see how it holds up: and while the shock factor is lessened when you know what to expect, the tension remains palpable and Navarrette’s transformation will age like wine.

In a world where all big studio movies are being lit like car commercials, it’s refreshing to see shadows used so effectively in a contemporary story. When Nikki’s face is obfuscated its not only good visual storytelling but also symbolically represents her dual personas.

Lastly, knowing Ian’s secret from the beginning shows his initial advice was not stupid but instead malicious. His actions initially seem as if he cares about Bear or Nicky’s wellbeing, but in actuality he was simply jealous and wanted his friend not to succeed.

My Original Review: Obsession

The raves about Inde Navarette are worth the hype, the comparisons to Pulse feel pretty overblown, and otherwise I think it’s… fine! Barker is clearly on his way to something, and that’s exciting to see. It’s also refreshing to see a flick chock full of social commentary on the evils of patriarchy without the need for a Big Speech to Explain the Theme. The story truly does the work to get you there, and it’s evident from start to stop exactly who the monster is and why.

That said, while it was a fine way to spend an afternoon, it’s not something that’s going to really stick with me or get much play. I think it’s an impressive debut for someone so young and I’m looking forward to seeing how he grows!

Isabelle Adjani in Possession, Toni Collette in Hereditary, and Kathy Bates in Misery are talked about as some of the best performances by women in horror movie history, and in my opinion, you can add Inde Navarrette to that list. The performance she gives here takes an already good movie and transcends it to another level. Her facial expressions, physical performance, and just how easily she's able to slip from being skin-crawlingly terrifying, darkly comedic, and completely sympathetic is a wonder to watch, and it will be a damn shame if she's not at least nominated for anything when awards season rolls around, because she's just that good. Curry Barker... You sicko! (Complimentary) I've watched Barker on YouTube for years, so it was awesome to see him make a feature-length studio movie, and he did a hell of a job here. Taking a classic "be careful what you wish for" story and spinning it into a modern tale of real love vs forced love, and balancing something so serious as consent and autonomy, while also being purposefully funny and delivering top-notch, unhinged scares all at the same time is impressive. Curry shows he has a deft hand at balancing wildly different tones in the same movie, and it still being a cohesive film that's firing on all cylinders, and I'll be excited about whatever he has coming in the future.

Honestly, Obsession was one of the biggest surprises of the year for me. I went into it without many expectations, and by the end I was genuinely impressed with what I had just watched. It takes a simple idea and turns it into something entertaining, weird, and completely unpredictable.

The story follows a man who desperately wants the woman he loves to love him back. It sounds like a simple premise, but the film keeps pushing that idea further until everything spirals into complete chaos. I really enjoyed how the story kept getting crazier without losing its focus.

One of my favorite parts was the comedy. The humor felt natural, and there were several moments that genuinely made me laugh. I wasn't expecting a horror film to be this funny, but the balance between comedy and horror worked surprisingly well.

The horror itself relies heavily on gore and violence, but it never felt excessive just for the sake of shocking the audience. Every brutal moment served the story and made the situation feel even more disturbing. That balance made the experience much more enjoyable.

The direction was another huge highlight. It's honestly hard to believe this film was made on a budget of around $750,000. The camera work, lighting, and overall presentation felt far bigger than its budget would suggest. You can tell the filmmakers knew exactly how to make the most of every dollar they had.

What impressed me even more is that the film became such a huge success despite its small budget. It proves that a strong idea and good execution can sometimes matter more than having a massive production.

By the end, I walked away having a great time. Obsession is funny, bloody, entertaining, and surprisingly creative. It was one of my favorite surprises of 2026, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys horror with dark comedy.

Cinema has always told stories of characters who embark on a mission to achieve some goal and make their desire come true, a desire that drives the story forward. It has also been able to demonstrate how treacherous and harmful this path can be. And it is from this premise that director Curry Barker begins in this Blumhouse film, almost a modern version of “The Chaser”, episode from "The Twilight Zone." Young Bear's seemingly genuine love for Nikki takes an even more sinister turn when she develops an unhealthy interest in him after the use of the mysterious "One-Wish Willow," a convenient MacGuffin that functions like an uncontrolled hormone or a date rape drug, a vile tool used by those who seek to obtain something without effort or effort. The film, in fact, literally takes on the form of a "rape and revenge" where a person's free will is violated and disrespected, without their consent. Male satisfaction and pride trump any natural feeling or apparent discomfort. Instinct prevails over everything, even reasoning. The toxicity of a forced relationship is seen and perceived by an unhealthy significant other who will prove to be a retaliation for the one who “took advantage” of her. The web of love slowly becomes a prison. The real image of a person literally disappears, replaced by the one that dwells in our subconscious, the one we think he wants and desires but who is actually dark and elusive like a "Hitchcockian ghost" transported to the Gen Z era, only more demonic (Nikki is just a black, empty, and indecipherable silhouette since we do not know the means to see it as it really is and that's how Barker chooses to represent her). And in the end, guilt, trauma, and her awareness reign supreme. Definitely one of the most "socially" disturbing horror films of the year.

Sue me: I like going to the AMC, eating popcorn, and chatting with my friends about new movies. But I don’t like it this much. I thought Keeper was the last straw—and it should’ve been—but no, it’s this. The genre has gone to a place that not even critical interest can carry me, so, unless there is a really good reason to do so, I will not be attending these movies anymore.

To prevent this experience from having been a total waste, I’ll attempt some summative comments on the “form” of these movies. Let’s start with a quote from director Curry Barker:

I wanted to shoot this center-composed and have extra head space because I wanted it to feel uncomfortable in its loneliness. There’s something about center-composed that forces you to look and pulls you in in a way that traditional composition may not. I’ve seen a lot of horror filmmakers I look up to recently shooting in that way.

The man lives by his words: nearly every shot in this film is center-framed with ample headspace (though not so ample as Lanthimos’ Killing of a Sacred Deer, which takes the conceit to an almost parodic extreme). Additionally, the majority of these compositions are lensed in shallow focus, meaning that, for the most part, only one object or person is clearly foregrounded in any given shot. A lot of these shots are medium close-ups, meaning that the object in question is usually just the actor’s face. And some of them even have zooms, as if the shallow focus and center framing were not sufficient emphases for whatever Mr. Barker is trying to draw our attention to.

Contra Mr. Barker, I would argue that the indifferent regularity of the center-framing produces an extremely comfortable spectatorial position—comfortable insofar as it is unvarying and predictable. The viewer’s eye never has to roam across the frame, and we never have to worry about where the point of interest in the next shot will be, because—bam!—there it is in the middle. The only exceptions are a few sub-Hereditary “figure in the background” shots, which invariably fall flat because constant shallow focus robs the frame of depth. The zooms conspire in the negation of depth too. Unlike track-in camera movements, where the camera actually pushes through the space, zooms flatten space by enlarging the composition from a static position. Far from “pulling you in”, these devices work hard to reduce the scope of the visual plain as much as possible. Each shot is a homogenous surface, structurally identical to the shots that precede and follow it, where we are immediately met with the “thing” we should be looking at.

The contrast Mr. Barker draws between his approach and “traditional composition” (what does he think that means?) is quite odd, because he is correct that an awful lot of horror filmmakers today are shooting their films the exact same way. This mode of composition has itself become such a “tradition” that it is no longer localized to a particular filmmaker or even studio: we tend to associate the inception of the approach with A24, but movies from Neon, Blumhouse, Focus Features, etc. have now gotten in on the game. Hereditary is plainly the benchmark that these movies strive to imitate. But Hereditary’s aesthetic approach (I have detailed it extensively here) was grounded in actual ideas, no matter how paltry they may have been; and moreover, for all his flaws, Aster does care about blocking the frame. By contrast, these filmmakers use this arsenal of tactics with little regard for the ideas they might convey or the emotional impact they have on the viewer. The primary motivation does not seem to be “discomfort” or “loneliness”, but simply an inability to stage action. You don’t have to stage action, to think about where to place the actor or the camera to communicate meaning, to contend with the multiple planes of depth within the frame when everything is stuck in the center! This aesthetic approach is a crutch that relieves the director from having even to attempt to stage action. And that is utterly fatal for horror, because horror depends on depth and action to facilitate tension. The viewer has to get the sense of an actual world where dangerous presences may be lurking, concealed, waiting to pounce. You don’t get that when you’ve ironed out every layer, every last vestige of visual complexity from your movie.The content feels almost irrelevant when the formal means through which that content is expressed are so self-defeating and hacky. Suffice to say that the narrative is extremely one-note, obvious from the get go, textureless, and makes use of such loathsome dramaturgical techniques as having the character explain their entire background and motivation explicitly in dialogue right at the start of the movie (another Hereditary holdover), deployment of dead animals to inflict pathos, following up horror gags with interminable constipated scenes wherein the characters recap what just happened and scream about how weird and fucked-up that was, totally uninteresting lore dumps, cheap shock tactics, and (inevitably) Aster-esque arbitrary cruelty, etc. The fact that such a paltry bag of tricks pushes two hours is an insult. It makes vulgar, reactionary schlock like Primate look like a model of economy and intrigue by comparison. At least that movie doesn’t wear its crude pleasures thin or weigh them down with undue, unearned portent.

For horror movies about the repression of the woman’s autonomy in patriarchal romance (and male guilt about same), the bifurcation of female consciousness, etc., please refer to Sisters, Audition, and Gone Girl. Those movies offer layered, intricate, and provocative explorations of the theme in question. They are also frightening, funny, and well-directed. I really don’t understand why anyone would accord a movie like Obsession the same level of esteem as those films, unless, of course, they happen to be one of those self-styled horror fans who indiscriminately embraces literally every genre movie they watch. But there aren’t many such people, are there?

One of the worst downstream effects of Wolf of Wall Street being basically the most important and influential movie of the 21st century is that its structure and moralizing has become thee fall-back for basically any story. This is because The Wolf of Wall Street is very popular, and very frequently mistaken for (pardon the context-sensitive double entendre) wish fulfillment. Thus, a lot of people over the years have been struck, when watching, by the realization that the film is a totalizing indictment of American capitalism and the way it warps how we talk to other people. It is a satire of all the things that it depicts. This clean binary framing is totally sound and so enticing. What if you show something in order to prove its opposite…the American public yearns for dialectics…

Anyway, a lot of movies these days function like this, presumably because it’s basically the only example of indirect form audiences will be trusted to understand. But if you’ll notice, we’ve sorta skipped something crucial about the movie in the above characterization. As part of Scorsese’s Catholic sense of sin, the film accepts that it is an advertisement for the very worldview it decries - that it will operate this way for many. This does not mean the film is a failure, but that Scorsese has accounted for, with total precision, the many ways his work will be misconstrued, and has made these readings crucial to examining the text itself. The film would not work if the lifestyle was not enticing!

Obsession is a WoWS-like. It is a movie where we see a thing happen, but only on the periphery. In this one, an insecure man accidentally robs a woman of her bodily autonomy to a supernatural degree, creating a misogynistic caricature that is ironically ruining his life, so he just kills himself to escape any culpability. It’s been extremely successful, because that’s a good premise, and a marketable premise. You can be woke or an incel and want to see that movie.

I like a mean movie, and this is mean, occasionally to great effect (the very ending surprised me in how perfectly it became the exact movie I’ve described above). But it is sloppy and uncommitted in ways I found really disappointing. Despite having been primed with all sorts of contradictory opinions, I was shocked by how many times it pulls its punches.

Fundamentally, the movie is not prepared to give incels their fantasy (and I do think this is an incel fantasy, and not about the allure of subtle misogyny, given how quickly Bear is deliberately 24/7 raping her). It does a really, really bad job of it! It sucks Bear doesn’t know his wish will come true! You can argue about whether or not, later on, he is being manipulative, but this kind of ambiguity is not really productive. It would be more effective to be clear, but Barker is 26 and this is his first movie and he doesn’t know how to write a woman speaking normally, let alone like some diatribe on abuse.

You can point out how we never truly see Nikki, how he reveals this pathetic, sadistic entitlement when she’s asleep, how much of the film is filtered through his eyes. But it’s not really prepared to suggest that using DARVO tactics might make Bear feel really good, that thinking of her as a pathological liar with BPD might turn him on, that his real fantasy might be ruining her. It is not confident enough to really commit to being evil enough to sell the depths of its depraved, roundabout empathy.

Comparisons between Inde Navarette and Madigan are overblown; The latter was approaching an old-form of hagsploitation extravagance with the grace of a Globe performer. Navarette is a green actress willing to make a lot of choices, many of which are good. But she still speaks her lines to a metronome like her fellow Gen-Z actors. She does sell all the best moments.

Otherwise, it is lit like shit and there’s nothing to look at in the first place, and the script is full of every telltale sign of a debut - from a wheel-spinning structure to clunky conversations that lean too hard on thin characters.

Worst of all is Nikki, though. She is just a major problem. She is never allowed to be a particularly compelling monster, because the film is too wishy-washy to let her ever be truly sidelined. It is terrifying to watch her be torn up inside. I was taken aback by how upsetting those first few minutes after the wish are…like she is slowly disassociating in ways that are first recognizable and then, steadily, supernatural.

But the pee on the floor, the mutilated corpse, the cat thing, the shot of Nikki’s vacant eyes as she gets fucked, that horrible fucking party scene….it’s allll over the place! Barker has made a film where, by design, Nikki must be a projection, and yet he has designed a creature feature where Nikki must be a spectacle. His approach ranges from absurd hijinx, to behavior with dubious connotations. It never really hits. I never want to be her, I'm never really scared of her, and I think he foregrounds the suffering of this poor girl on way too much for a movie where she will inherently be unknowable.

Anyway, this movie depressed me and nagged at me, because I think it makes the least interesting choice nine times out of ten. I was expecting to be offended or secretly delighted. I was mostly frustrated. I don’t think you’re evil or stupid for liking this, but even in the most neutral terms, I was often struggling to care about its bullshit. I have deliberately avoided describing all the other ways one could go with this exact premise (imagine the pro-polyamory version of this…) because I wanted to meet it on its own terms, accept that this was an examination of Gen-Z heterosexual violences and that it was focused on subverting the vessel, nothing more. Even on those generous/narrow terms, Obsession failed me.

The hype surrounding this movie has been unreal, and that can always go one of two ways: either it lives up to expectations or it crashes under them. Luckily, this one firmly falls into the first category. From the very beginning, the film does a fantastic job introducing its antagonist—and yes, I’m calling him the villain; I don’t care what anyone says. This is a man who has absolutely no idea what he wants out of life. I’ve seen people label him a “nice guy,” an “incel,” and all sorts of things, but honestly I don’t think he fully fits any of those categories because that would require him to actually commit to being something. My dude can’t decide on anything. The man can’t even choose the right words. The second he said “more than anything in the world,” I knew things were about to spiral. Let this film be a warning to always measure your words carefully because you never know when one sentence is going to ruin your life. And honestly, when the girl you’re obsessed with literally has “Freaky” in her nickname, maybe take that as another giant warning sign.

Curry Barker does a masterful job building tension almost immediately. There’s this deeply unsettling atmosphere hanging over the entire film, amplified by the effective score that constantly reminds you something is very, very wrong. The horror leans more into dread and psychological discomfort than straight-up scares, though there’s one sequence in a car that genuinely freaked the living hell out of me. The entire third act is devilishly effective and fully commits to the bleakness the movie has been building toward from the start. There’s also a surprisingly good amount of dark humor sprinkled throughout, adding brief moments of levity without ever undercutting the horror.

I’ll admit I was a little skeptical after hearing all the overwhelming praise Inde Navarrette was getting, especially the Oscar talk. For a good chunk of the runtime I wasn’t fully convinced, but as the film progressed she completely won me over. Her performance becomes increasingly unhinged while still feeling painfully human. She doesn’t play Nicky as a straightforward monster or villain, but rather as a deeply broken soul who seems trapped in some incomprehensible nightmare. She feels less possessed and more imprisoned inside her own personal hell. I especially loved the small moments where the “real” Nicky briefly resurfaces — confused, frightened, desperate. In a twisted sort of way, I actually felt sorry for her. Navarrette’s physical performance is fantastic too. The way she contorts her body and moves throughout the film becomes genuinely disturbing, like you’re witnessing a human being slowly transform into something monstrous. The manic laughter, the emoji sad face, all those tiny gestures filled with nuance really elevate the performance.

All in all, this is horror executed in a way that feels genuinely stressful and deeply uncomfortable. I can’t remember the last time a horror film made me feel this consistently uneasy. Even when I had a feeling where things were heading, the movie never lost its grip on me. I was locked into my seat the entire time. If Curry Barker keeps delivering work at this level, he’s got an incredibly promising career ahead of him.

A great deal of this rating is for Inde Navarrette's wildly unnerving performance as Nikki, who loses her identity in big bites when her bestie, cute and accommodating sad boy Bear, uses a surprisingly real wish to make her love him more than anyone else. Barker smartly does not allow even a wisp of gratification to come out of this wish fulfillment, smothering out the allure, satisfaction, and thrill of romance and sex through music, sound design, and, mostly, Navarrette's striking facial contortions and physical control. Barker knows the premise is thin and rather than take a risk and break out of its dramatic boundaries, he cleverly finds ways to up the ante in timid and miniscule ways every 15-20 minutes until it hits its obvious conclusion, which makes much of the action of the second half to feel droning as we approach that climax. The more egregious limitations, however, can be found in the writing, as much as the visual Aster-K. Kurosawa fanboying began to gnaw at me around the midway point. As critical as the film can get of Bear, neither Michael Johnston's performance nor Barker's writing of Bear is as nasty as this sickening story calls for. In fact, there are multiple unconvincing attempts to juice sympathy for this contemptible and pathetic person in the film. For all the self-infliction that goes into what Bear's wish puts him through, the film ultimately can't help but frame him as a victim of sorts, which directly goes against the best ideas Barker offers here. The truth of the matter is that this is Nikki's story, and the insistence on making it a movie about the tragedy of poor, immature Bear makes this an increasingly losing proposition as it goes on, even if this is meant to be proof that Barker is in on the quite obvious joke. Instead of focusing on the genuinely eerie and dramatically robust experience of Nikki in being supernaturally forced to lose control of her emotional world through the childish act of a man she unfortunately trusted and loved, the writer-director engineers Nikki to be little more than the delivery system for the film's scares, shocks, and gross-outs. That Navarette is nevertheless still able to carve out a slim yet staggering portrait of gutting betrayal and horrific, helpless manipulation is a testament to the talent of the performer and, up to a point, her writer-director.

Obsession absolutely rocks. What a wild and unique take on a concept that could have easily fallen into familiar territory. It all starts with Inde Navarrette, who shows an insane amount of range, delivering strong physicality and putting us through plenty of mental turmoil. Curry Barker’s attention to detail is integral, as he nails everything from the lighting to his clever use of camera angles. The film often feels more uncomfortable than scary, which isn’t inherently bad, but the inclusion of humor and intentionally cringe-worthy moments makes up for the occasional lack of depth. The end result is an insanely entertaining time at the theater… What a ride.

Watching Obsession felt like playing Silent Hill 2 for the first time; somehow productive in its misery, i feel like both works highlight an aspect of cruelty we don't often see in media.

Yes, "Nikki" was technically only present for a fraction of the films runtime; the lion's share of Inde's stellar performance went to whatever entity was residing within her body and interacting with Bear and everyone else in this town.

In Silent Hill, I think of Maria's narrative function as the "projection" from which James' supplants his more possessive and lewd desires, while in Obsession, Nikki is on the receiving end of Bears projections of "love" or affection in a way that the entity only seems to propagate her behavior based on how Bear is willing to receive it.

It reminds me that in any scene where Bear is conflicted about bringing Nikki back, or in his unwillingness to act sooner on her captivity (within her own body) that i think we learn a lot about this movie's sentiment towards unrequited love, that people without the ability to choose or navigate intimacy without full autonomy are subjected not only to the potential cruelty of someone else's desires, but also to feel as within and without one's own skin.

Perhaps the most meaningful aspect to me was walking out of the theater and hearing how many people were bustling about how Bear was such a rotten fellow. Just like James Sunderland, gaming's most wretched scumbag.

If Silent Hill 2 is my favorite thing ever, Obsession is certainly my favorite thing right now. Bravo Curry Barker, bravo Inde Navarrette, will be watching again and again

this pretty viscerally upset me in ways that few movies ever have, and I've still been feeling the panic and anxiety in my body the next day. overall, I think that's a compliment; this is a truly frightening experience in a way that few horror films have ever been for me, and as a directorial debut (and a staggering performance showcase) it deserves flowers by the truckload.

still, I'm left wrestling with the emotional takeaway of the film. obviously, the whole thing clearly reads as a commentary on young men who see a woman's love as fundamentally owed to them by birthright, even when they're too cowardly to voice their feelings for themselves. and for any moderately intelligent viewer, I think it's very overt that Bear (clever choice of name) is "the real villain" here; yes, he didn't know the wish was real until it worked, but even when he discovers for a fact that the true Nikki is suffering torturously, he merely tries to alter the wish to tamp down its effects and then gets defensive ("what's so bad about being with me?") when she begs him for help. even in his final moments, he's too much of a coward to truly make the "heroic" self-sacrificial choice and tries to vomit the pills up instead. he's pathetic, and intentionally so. the film is also fairly applicable, I think, to the increasing prevalence of AI "relationships"—one-sided dynamics where a person (usually, a lonely guy) literally generates a partner whose sole purpose is to affirm them and serve their every desire with no agency or interiority.

that's all well and good and admirable as a commentary. but I think what's leaving me a little bit uneasy is the way that despite the obviousness of Bear as the perpetrator and despite the way it clearly empathizes with the tragedy of Nikki's fate, I'm still left feeling like the "psycho girlfriend as the horror movie monster" premise nonetheless leaves the audience with the emotional experience of fear and alienation toward a helpless woman. especially in the film's most intense moments, despite your intellectual knowledge that Bear is the problem, Nikki is so terrifying that you almost want to see him physically "defend himself" from her. emotionally, if not intellectually, the film largely puts the audience in Bear's shoes—shoes which inherently degrade Nikki. and the fact that the only other female character in the film meets such a gruesome and dehumanizing end (at the hands of another woman pitted against her, no less) is deeply upsetting and cruel, even if it's "supposed" to be.

looking down at the rows in front of me during my screening, I could see several groups of teenage boys—many of whom pointed and laughed at various things between each other throughout. when the credits rolled, I couldn't help but ask myself: are those boys going to walk away from this experience thinking, "I should be more careful about treating women as though they owe me their love"? Or are they merely going to turn to each other and say, "bro, it would be scary to have a girlfriend like that"? I don't know.

I'm probably being a little too fun-police toward interpretation here, and maybe my version of things would be too didactic. I don't think it's a storyteller's responsibility to "make" every audience member "get it," and many of the films that most aggressively critique things like toxic masculinity (like Fight Club) have still been misconstrued by morons to mean the opposite of what their creators intended. that's out of anyone's hands, and I'm glad to see these ideas explored onscreen with some degree of thoughtfulness, even when it's clumsy. still, stories and images have power, and I can't help but wonder how the broader culture of young people will receive this one in spirit, even if the text is ostensibly trying to subvert the psycho-girlfriend trope with something more compassionate. I mean, compassionate is not exactly how I’d describe the film’s scene-to-scene feeling. I guess the short version is, I respect everything the movie is going for, but does it accomplish it? I'm not sure. I don't think the movie as it stands is lacking in empathy for Nikki, but it's interesting to imagine a version with more interiority afforded to her—especially since she is experiencing the truest horror in the story. and as much as I'm impressed with Curry Barker's creativity, I can't help but wonder what a woman would have done differently with similar material.

as an addendum: another reason that this movie affected me on a deep level was that I've known a couple of people in my life over the years with BPD who did not get the help that they needed. as much as I empathized with Nikki, I also couldn't help but feel the helplessness in some of those unpredictable moments of erratic behavior where you're left trying to placate another person's traumatic episode and figure out what's wrong until it ends with a disorienting snap out of it and dramatic apologies and suddenly it's like it never even happened. the moments of self-harm and the bedroom scene in the middle of the night, in particular, felt immediately vivid and intimately distressing to me; I almost felt like I was going to cry. in that way, I think the universal emotions the film taps into can be very, very, very real in the lives of many people, and that works in its advantage. whether those very real people's experiences deserve to be used as a horror device, or whether the depiction nonetheless actually offers resonant representation anyway, I'm not totally sure. on the BPD reddit, there seems to be a mix of people finding it stereotypical and others feeling profoundly seen by it. it hit me hard regardless! and I'll probably be digesting and making sense of the whole experience for a long time. that's the best and worst thing I can say right now.

She’s genuinely on another level of craziness here with a ton of memorable moments. Her character of the beautiful Nikki Freeman made for something that I won’t be able to get out of my head for at least a couple of weeks. From her facial expressions, acting mentally batshit crazy in such a conveying manner, to jump scares that actually got me and straight up disturbing walking movements, I was completely floored. Whatever this actress does next, regardless of the genre, I’ll simply be seated for, and I was kind of left thinking by the end of this that she would have been the perfect choice for the upcoming Possession remake. Michael Johnston played this manipulative character of Bear in such a great way to the point where I had no idea how far his actions could go. It made the backwards half of this film not only effective but satisfying, with the dynamic and chemistry between the two actors making this something real special, at least in my personal opinion.

I was almost nervous that Obsession was going to end abruptly, but Curry Barker managed to stick the landing with an ending that couldn’t have been more perfect, in my opinion.

Obsession is simply a very good horror film, with a basic concept executed really well. It is obviously disturbing but also quite funny. The story is a classic variation of a Monkey's Paw premise, filtered through a modern lens of dating anxiety and loss of consent. As a horror film it both pleased the sick little freak in me that can admire pitch black comedy and also repulsed me in how dark a path the lead goes down. There is a slight Audition vibe to Obsession, given the film is about a performance of love which sits atop a more twisted tale that can be placed between displaying and critiquing misogyny, before giving way to unpredictable nasty violence. Though Obsession feels much more shallow. It rides on the stylistic clichés of the previous decade of acclaimed Hollywood horror, without bringing many original ideas to the table. Yet that doesn't really matter, because Obsession gets the basics right. It balances both a terrifying and comedic tone, it has well written characters who allow the horror around them to feel organic, and it manages to unsettle consistently. Obsession is just very solid, with effective filmmaking and a compelling story. It's a fascinating blend of established ideas, made with a restraint and confidence that suits it very well.

A horror movie that contains shades of Sorry, Baby with how it’s able to balance tone in spite of some of the material being incredibly heavy.

Obsession is working with a premise that’s very simple on paper. What if a timid young man who never had the guts to voice his allegedly strong feelings, was handed the woman who was the focal point of his obsession? How would he feel if the person who he’s built his entire existence around, built their entire existence around him?

Michael Johnston plays Bear’s quiet cowardice perfectly, while Indie Navarrette flat out gives one of the best performances of the year thus far, stealing the show at every turn. Nikki presents as a fairly normal girl next door, but through the terrifying power of the One Wish Willow becomes trapped in a prison of her own mind. The Nikki that we come to know is a shell of her actual self, moving and speaking like an AI system that’s struggling to reboot.

The implications here are obviously heinous, and the film knows when to stop being coy and directly address the knowledge that Bear possesses and his true character as a wolf in sheep’s clothing. While some moments here are jaw-droppingly upsetting, Curry is able to flip a switch and move into comedy with ease. Ian and Sarah are each great characters for the story to bounce off of as needed, but this is the Nikki and Bear show through and through.

The film is more than capably shot, with an aspect ratio change that actually serves the narrative and drives Curry’s point home. The sound design is piercing, rattling the audience to their core when needed. Obsession refuses to allow you to get comfortable, and refuses to allow you to stop thinking about the thematic material presented as well. Great film, make the time for it!

Desire as violation. Desperate yearning mutated into something parasitic and grotesque. The terrifying realization that being “wanted” and being “seen” are not remotely the same thing.

Obsession is the kind of horror film that leaves you feeling “spiritually” contaminated. The kind that violently rips through your skin, crawls beneath, and lingers there like rot. The kind that distorts familiar emotional terrain–unrequited love, longing for connection–into an insidious, uncompromising, waking nightmare.

For me, writer-director Curry Barker achieves cinematic perfection here thanks to 5️⃣ key factors:

🔑 Barker crafts a cautionary “be careful what you wish for” tale with ample meat and bones and gnashing teeth. This is a relentlessly vicious interrogation of romantic entitlement, dependency, and a range of unintended consequences (and unseen burdens) rooted in treating love like something owed or controllable.

🔑 This film possesses a brilliant tonal balance where awkward humor, aching vulnerability, surreal dread, tenderness, and pure, uncut nightmare fuel all harmoniously coexist.

🔑 I love the portrayal of Bear's character and his response to the predicament that he recklessly created. He's somewhat sympathetic (to a point) but also deeply frustrating. He's vulnerable and insecure (and recognizable) but also self-pitying and suffers from low-grade selfishness that's part and parcel of "nice guy" entitlement. He isn't the victim. Nikki is. Bear considers himself a “decent” guy, and (I guess) he strives to be most of the time - aside from him seemingly being allergic to taking accountability. 😏

🔑 All the performances delivered the goods (Michael Johnston was great as Bear!), but this is truly the Inde Navarrette show. She delivers one of the most impressively unsettling horror performances that I’ve ever seen. The specific way she oscillates between tenderness, desperation, emotional terror, and unhinged devotion is phenomenal. There’s a suffocating intensity to her performance that makes even moments of “affection” feel threatening.

🔑 For me, what makes the horror in Obsession so uniquely exceptional is the emotional and “spiritual” implications underpinning the carnage and tainted love.

Emotionally, every horrific escalation feels tethered to emotional deterioration, relational collapse, and psychological erosion. We witness how desire disconnected from empathy warps into something predatory. Possessive. Consumptive. Monstrous.

(⚠️Spoiler alert‼️)“Spiritually,” we know that this is not what Real Nikki wants. Wish Nikki behaves the way she does because love stripped of agency and consent is necessarily inhuman. Wish Nikki's merely a humanoid vessel for desires, the human embodiment of planted intrusive thoughts that were never conjured by Real Nikki to begin with. And as Wish Nikki acts out this mutilated, corrosive species of all-consuming love for Bear, Real Nikki is supplanted, damned to a form of psychical imprisonment and existential annihilation akin to Get Out's sunken place. 😱

Be careful what you wish for because Obsession takes that idea and turns it into something genuinely disturbing. This is easily one of the most uncomfortable films I have seen this year and I could not and I mean could not look away.

A hopeless romantic uses something called the one wish willow to make his crush fall in love with him and once that happens the film just spirals fast.

What the film is really getting at is the difference between love and control. It starts from something relatable wanting to be loved and being afraid of rejection. But than it pushes that into something dangerous. Because once you take away someone's choice it's not love anymore its possession.

Which that is where the horror really hits you. Watching someone slowly lose themselves until there not even a person anymore just someone shaped to fit someone else's desire.

By the end I was just sad because it all comes back to loneliness and what happens when love turns into something that consumes instead of connects.

Overall. Obsession is one of the most disturbing horror films of the year. It turns loneliness, rejection, and obsession into something emotionally exhausting and genuinely unsettling. Inde Navarrette delivers a chilling performance that makes the film's themes about love, control, and losing your identity hit even harder.

A word-of-mouth phenomenon like OBSESSION is bound to have its virtues and flaws exaggerated. In the former category, director Curry Barker achieves a sustained mood of unease, although this isn’t entirely to his credit. The choice to mine tension from long static takes that focus on a central point, usually the silhouette of lead Inde Navarette, or a window through which she might appear to raise hell, in tandem with his background in horror sketches, give the proceedings a tempo of slow builds and short shocks while disguising many formal deficiencies. Outside of the dramatic lighting scheme, little attention has been paid to composition, particularly noticeable in the handful of clumsy daytime setups. Navarette’s performance, on the other hand, has allowed many critics to praise the film as a flawed vehicle for her tour de force, which is yet another sleight of hand working to obfuscate a troubling concept. Playing the dream girl whose personality and actions are directed by a monkey’s-paw curse, the destructive potential of Navarette’s figure lies mostly offscreen, the better to serve Barker’s narrative structure, which means that the camera’s infatuated gaze lingers on the spectacle of her helpless abnegation, in a key scene returning to find her covered in sick like an ill housepet. The many shortcomings of the script (whose “critique” of incel ideology has been wildly overstated by a film media credulous of overnight success stories) and the other performances do little to counter the impression of women as dependent and wasteful animals, or of heterosexual relations as a zero-sum death trap, ideas which whether consciously expressed or not make this feature an authentically upsetting diversion. Against these charges, the strongest argument in Barker’s defense might be that his debut is less skillfully or intentionally crafted than partisans would admit.

I'm exhausted. I've U-Hauled twice in three months. Ran myself ragged apartment searching. About to start a job that'll test my trucking skills beyond anything before. I've been making full use of my brief enforced unemployment too: I'm training for a triathlon; I'm contra-dancing; I'm taking tennis lessons.

In short, life's been good... and also too much. That's how it should be, more or less, I think.

So, with my head being where it's at lately, what exactly am I looking for in a movie? On the one hand, escapism, for my exhausted senses; on the other hand, something meaningful to chew on, to help make sense of my life. Such is the tension inherent in cinema itself -- and, when properly faced, a good, productive tension.

The worst thing, then, is for a film to be neither fish nor fowl. Unfortunately, that's what we get here. One more in the growing modern horror sub-animalistic-cheap-thrills-and-gross-out-spectacle-with-a-message-wrapped-in-a-bow genre. Where even the sensory thrills are ineptly framed, ineptly paced, ineptly assembled. If I must be charitable, I might say that it at least made me feel appropriately grossed out by the moral turpitude of the male lead, that Inde Navarette’s character work at least evoked some twinge in the pit of my gut; but that kind of faint praise is more insulting than criticism.

It is not hard at all in the darkened cinema-hall, with my nose pressed up against the giant screen in seat A1 and the subwoofer thudding through my skull, for a film to churn my stomach. But simply striking repeated dull blows on the same few sore spots of the body, the dead spot of the eyeball especially (center framing) – which kills the free play of the audience’s gaze and turns it into a fatiguing test of endurance – has nothing to do with the art of horror: the art of misdirecting, not on the axis of soft <--> LOUD or normal <--> SCARY, but on the axis of desire <--> revulsion. The dialectic of it: how we desire what repulses us and hate what we desire (translated of course into the concrete language of montage with the interplay of all five sense-elements). That is the baseline of horror as a genre; any movie without it is not worth the label.

The most frustrating thing is that the premise seems to promise the sort of juicy psychoanalysis that’s an eternal wellspring for the genre. The “Nice Guy” softboi, with his pretend sensitivity, thinks he wants love; but confronted by the too-muchness of jouissance, neither able to embrace fulfillment, nor being selfless enough to renounce it, instead transmutes this seemingly noble feeling into sado-masochism. We’ve seen many examples of this in the genre, not just in the greatest works but even in passable mass-or-middlebrow art. It’s not exactly uncharted territory.

Unfortunately, director Curry Baker doesn’t even seem to have any interest in this 101-level psychoanalysis; I doubt he even knows what psychoanalysis is. Michael Johnston’s artless bag of nervous tics, his tiresome hemming and hawing and wincing, does not modulate whatsoever in either amplitude or implication. There is no sado-masochism on display, no real drive on the narrative’s part to plumb the contradictions of the lead’s desires. A director with guts would have had part of this character secretly relish (and I don’t mean in abstract dialogue, but actual embodied action) the power he has over his girlfriend. The very same clinginess on her part that scares the shit out of him should also turn him on, at the same time. Instead, he cowers before his wish-fulfillment for the entire groaning 2 hours. He is simply a Soft Boy Who’s Too Sensitive To Express Himself, And Maybe A Little Indecisive, And Can You Really Blame Him For Not Understanding That Magic Is Real? He Didn’t Mean It, Deep Down. Even the way he blurts out the wish before breaking the twig felt like a two-second chore to get out of the way, with no real longing behind it. When you boil it down, it ends up absolving masculinity under the guise of weak-ass “critique”.

(Sidebar on the weak-ass “one-wish willow” prop: I cannot stress how much of a nothing prop that was. And in the Monkey-Paw Subgenre of horror, you simply cannot afford to have the Monkey-Paw be a nothing prop, as a matter of basic competence! Seriously, just compare with – for a low-brow example – say, the Zoltar Machine in Tom Hanks’ Big with its unabashedly magical orientalist design; or – for a high-brow example – say, the cigarette lighter in Cure, where the unassuming normalcy of the prop is given an estranged halo through the art of montage. Here again, form = content: the weak-ass “one-wish willow” prop is simply a reflection of the weak-ass (non)interrogation of male desire. And don’t give me none of that “well he’s using a mundane prop to reflect the mundanity of modern woo-woo spirituality”. Please. This shit’s not smart enough for that, be real.)

And, despite the valiant efforts on actress Inde Navarrette’s part to give flesh and nuance to her character (her stage name is, to get psychoanalytic once again, almost a subconscious linguistic screen for “Indie Narrative”... that’s all I’ll say on that), unfortunately, the writing and directing just isn’t there for her to hang her work on. There’s nothing she can do to humanize her character in those scenes where her face (save for perhaps a pair of spectrally glowing eyes) is shrouded in suffocating shadow, where the director clearly treats her more as an apparition, a fleshless symbol, a mere projection of the man’s psychology, than a properly human character. The one instance where her “true self” breaks through to beg for a mercy kill is completely unearned because of the total lack of buildup. There is no sense of who she is as a personality before the magic took hold of her, so therefore there can be no sense of a struggle between her autonomous being and the encroaching alien obsession.

The real horror of love, our fear of the murky boundary between genuine care and obsession, is precisely in the not-knowing of where exactly the line is. The terror of losing oneself in love, of wanting to be good for one’s partner and yet turning (despite one’s best efforts) into a monster, is one of the truest fears out there. Not the slightest curiosity about exploring that here: the character’s obsession simply seizes hold of her from the outside, mechanically; with its inner logic following, not the desires of a real woman (which a good horror film would then exaggerate and contort but without ever losing sight of the inner logic), but a collection of Men’s Worst Fears Of What A Clingy Girlfriend Would (Stereotypically) Act Like. Is it any surprise that this pulls the same old shit of killing the men characters with gentle gunshots and the women characters with violent face-smashes?

When I decided I wanted to start dancing socially, I ended up choosing contra dance because I have, I’m ashamed to say, two left feet. (Even Jo, the sweet old grandma who tried to teach me a proper contra swing – a contra swing is the easiest swing there is in existence – had to give up.) The beauty of contra is that one can walk all of the moves if must be. In other words, there are no steps, only figures. A perfect dance form for people with two left feet. (One of the few things you gotta hand to white culture – they understand the barrier of entry for a casual social dance shouldn’t be Grandmaster level!)

What that means is that, when I’m walking a swing with a partner who’s just here to chill, I will simply take one step per beat, like a normal walk; and when I’m swinging a partner who actually wants to swing, well, I have to make do with frantically catching up with their pace with stutter steps, like a graceless geisha’s.

It’s a good way to have a fun time, but not exactly aesthetic for bystanding voyeurs.

All this is to say, this lack of rhythm, this rudimentary tempo of plodding and frantic steps, without dimensionality, texture or proper modulation, is an exact analogy for the effect had by the formal language dissected by Brian’s review. When film theorists were first conceptualizing montage, they thought of each shot (naively) as a sort of ideogram, a collection of which would be strung together the way words string together into a sentence. Of course they quickly learned that this conception was wrong-headed; that what made film unique, its capturing of Concrete Presence rather than Symbol, made this film-as-verbal-language model obsolete, or at least more complicated.

But they still retained the concept of montage. They did, however, expand its meaning. Not the simplistic trick of “close up of man’s face + insert of bowl of soup = hungry”, but the complex, holistic interplay of image, words, sound, action, character, color, shape, line, motion, time – in short, every element of the five senses, conceived not as symbol but as concrete presence – and their collaboration and contrast.

It seems as if, in this current visual diet dominated by TikTok sketches, YouTube video essay, and Twitch streams, the instincts of so many younger filmmakers are reverting to the old “ideogram” model, but on an infinitely more impoverished level. The young Eisenstein was at least experimenting in virgin territory, and his ideograms (before he abandoned that method in maturity) were far from cliches, but were odd, sharp, jarring symbols seen from angles no human eye had seen before; our current generation of directors’ ideograms are floating heads speaking baldly in extreme shallow focus, or else the first concept that comes to mind. Girl = ghost? Put her in shadow.

The culmination of this is the total breakdown of space – and with that, any sense of real haunting. Ideograms simply cannot scare anyone deep down. In one of the shot-reverse-shots, which the director clearly meant to be proud of as a plot hinge, we see the male lead’s horrified face. Cut to what he was reacting to: revealed for the first time, his girlfriend had taped his front door shut with comical amounts of duct tape. It was clearly meant to evoke a mix of horror and nervous laughter; yet the audience (who did respond to the other, more gross-out but less meaningful spectacle) did not react at all to this key moment.

The reason? The shot-reverse-shot was cut together axially, at exactly 180 degrees. In other words, there was zero overlap in mise-en-scene between one shot and the next. We don’t have a man discovering a horrifying mass of lumpy tape protruding into the same space that he is in. We have a picture of a man, and a picture of the tape, side by side like a Powerpoint slideshow. How can this scare anyone? At most, it’ll allow one to intellectually register what’s going on (“oh, that’s what the director is trying to say – I might not feel it, but I can at least see that he is doing it”) and then move on, and the image leaves no imprint.

That’s not cinema.

I don’t know what the solution is, but it certainly can’t be the current “indie” environment where every young filmmaker is expected to have an easily identifiable, “branded” style, which can be manifest in every single shot (shaped by an unvarying mold lest anyone miss the “branding”) – that style then being simply overlaid on undigested “narrative”. From what I hear about film labs at places like Sundance, it seems like 99% of what young filmmakers workshop there is this undigested narrative, spruced up with some “character work” and “dialogue work” and such, and then a little bit of discussion on how to “realize” this narrative “visually”, and that’s it.

Maybe what we really need is a renewed apprenticeship in the basic building blocks of montage. Forget narrative, learn how to cut “meaningless” sounds and images together pleasingly, with a sense of tempo and texture. Do that for a few years, then we’ll be ready to tell stories… I don’t know. Worth a try.

If I’m being honest, it can get a bit tiring to bring up Hereditary every time a new horror movie drops that feels even slightly ambitious. “Does it reach Hereditary levels?” has become this exhausting reflex. However, there’s a reason it keeps happening. When Ari Aster’s movie came out, it scared people but it also felt like it rewrote the rules. It showed that horror could be this raw, psychologically devastating family drama wrapped in supernatural dread, with craftsmanship that rivaled prestige dramas. It became the new blueprint.

After watching Obsession, I’m starting to wonder if we’re on the cusp of another shift.

If you had told me this was Curry Barker’s feature debut, I wouldn’t have believed you. The guy moves like a veteran. The lighting is so precise and moody, the tension builds in these slow, suffocating layers that make your shoulders stay tense for the whole runtime, and the way he blends genuinely funny, awkward comedic moments into a story that gradually becomes horrifying is masterful.

There were several moments where I was legitimately stressed out because I genuinely had no idea what was coming next, especially with Inde Navarrette’s character, Nikki. She’s unpredictable in the best (and most terrifying) way. Navarrette gives one of the best performances I’ve seen all year. She sinks her teeth into this role and doesn’t let go. There’s this unhinged energy mixed with vulnerability that makes Nikki feel dangerously real. You’re invested in her from the jump, and that emotional hook is what elevates the whole thing.

This is one of those movies that demands more than one viewing. I caught it at a screening with a Q&A afterwards, and the cast and director dropped some details I completely missed the first time. There’s a lot to unpack here as well: obsession and desire, the blurred lines between love and control, the way our best intentions can twist into something nightmarish.

If Curry Barker keeps making movies at this level, he’s going to be a household name in the horror genre for years to come. The man has the vision, the technical skill, and the understanding of what makes an audience squirm and laugh in equal measure. After Obsession, I’m genuinely excited for whatever he does next. The horror genre feels like it’s in really good hands right now.

Not sure why I want to go to bat for this one, especially when a lot of people I like and respect seem intent on taking a bat to it. One reason is because the reflexive embrace of so much recent horror has precipitated some equally reflexive skepticism ( I promise you, mutuals, I’m not talking about you personally). Another is because I’ve now seen Obsession twice – once at a press screening and once with friends who aren’t critics, or even genre fans (self-described or otherwise) – and think it to be, as they say, a rich text. Leaving aside Curry Barker’s content-creator bona fides, his Gen-Z pedigree, and the less-than-inspiring thrust of his interviews – he’s been doing a lot of them, which is what happens when you make a big hit like this –and also the fact that fear factor, like laughter, is 1) subjective and 2) involuntary, meaning that I will take those who didn’t find Obsession funny and/or scary (in equal measure or at all) at their word and in good faith, I’m compelled by the filmmaker’s decision to never let us Nikki except through Bear’s eyes (with one irritating, and maybe unfortunately telling exception, which I’ll get to later).

I’ve seen the opening scene, in which Bear rehearses coming clean about his submerged crush with a waitress on her work break, described as an exposition dump, and so it is. It’s also funny, insofar as it suggests that Nikki – or Not-Nikki, as it turns out – is basically inter-changable as far as Michael, and the movie that shares his POV, beginning with these literal-POV shots, is concerned. Not that Nikki could literally be anyone, but that Bear is mostly projecting loneliness and need onto another party (“when I moved here, you were the first person who was nice to me”), which sets the tone for what is pretty obviously a movie about – if not capital-A About – a pernicious form of nice-guy entitlement. I don’t know if Barker has much to say on the subject. But I do think he opens the can of worms and gropes around inside it, and that Nikki’s lack of definition pre-possession is part of that squirmy mandate.

For instance: Nikki never shares her writing with Bear; we only see her handing money to a homeless person from over his shoulder; the framing keeps decapitating her or rendering her in silhouette before the wish gets made. Even if to some extent these choices point towards a lack of imagination or curiosity on the filmmaker’s part –towards a fairly typical case of a writer-director drawing a blank and calling it portraiture – it surely serves the overall and insidious solipsism of the material. We’re all willing to varying degrees to forgo/forgive disparities in evident or on-the-record artistic intent for movies we like and use them as a smoking gun to indict the ones we don’t, and that’s OK; I say that whatever juice Obsession has trickles forth from its inversion of the study invasion-of-the-body-snatcher trope whereby we’re keenly aware of what – or who – has been lost in the process.

Nikki is a cipher precisely because Bear doesn’t really know her, which in turn gives the moments where her submerged consciousness suddenly emerges (and look, the logic of these beats, and of the One-Wish-Willow in general, is dubious) a little bit of friction. (Inde Navarette is especially good at inhabiting what may be Nikki's received, subliminal *idea* of what dream-girl deference could look or sound like; her performance is at its best when her character is also performing ). Ditto Bear’s response to Nikki’s sleep-talking explanation that they’ve actually never been together, which is to revert to the same self-pitying, smol-bean tone of the opening scene and ask her if it really would have been so bad to have been with him in the first place.

That question comes from a dark place, and however Barker has accessed it – through callowness or calculation or an understanding of how to twist the proverbial knife – I’ve been affected by it two times now. The rest of it – the glib hand-waving away of magic-realist absurdities; the head-smashing obviousness of the head-smashing set piece; the weirdly haphazard staging of the finale – is whatever, mileage may vary. As for that irritating and maybe telling exception, it’s a terrible mistake to hold on Nikki frozen mid-smile after Bear opens the duct-taped front door (funny) and leaves for work; it reminded me of the (terrifying) bit in Paranormal Activity where Katie stands beside the bed, and how it’s shown to us in fast-forward, via surveillance footage.

There’s no corollary to that objective gaze in Obsession, and considering that the scariest stuff is all synced to what Bear sees and hears (I really do like the phone call to/from Hell), Barker could have been more rigorous. He could have done a lot of things, I guess; he did enough for me, anyway.

With peace and love, I have no idea what’s going on with the love for this movie. It’s... really bad? On a writing and directing level, this movie feels like it was made by high schoolers. Everything is so amateurishly cobbled together and scattershot, to a point where it’s almost shocking it was released like this. Decisions as simple as where the camera is, when a cut is made, or where a scene starts or ends so regularly feel unintentionally bizarre and ill-fitting. It mistakes being LOUD for being effective, when so often all it has to lean back on is “oh my god isn’t she SO CRAZY?!?!”

The sad thing is that there’s actually some decent threads that could be pulled on and followed here. When it’s most effective is the moments where we see Nikki’s actual consciousness trying breaking through. Credit to Inde Navarrette who, let’s be clear, is phenomenal across this whole movie, and not only far and away the best part of it, but also the only reason why anything about it that works does work at all. The shimmers where we’re able to get windows into her perspective are harrowing, but that never really feels like the perspective through which. this film was envisioned, and the lens it was built from isn’t even dug into beyond the most rudimentary observations.

There’s nothing remotely terrifying about the litany of “oh she’s so weird” shallow monotony Barker employs, nor the irritatingly vacuous shock value being hammered in. But what is genuinely unnerving is when we’re forced to reckon with the real human being who is lost and confused and afraid in there. Who has no idea what’s happening to her, and at a certain point is simply begging to be put out of her misery. That’s where the human toll of this story comes into play, and Navarrette really raises that above what’s on the page to make it land.

On the counter, the entirety of what’s going on with Bear is kind of a disaster. We never get much of a sense of the inner life of this guy. Not before the wish, but also not even after. Scenes with him just drone on with him giving the same sort of blank or freaked out expression, but it feels torturous wanting to know more about what he’s actually thinking or feeling beyond “this is so weird.” Unfortunately that seems to be where the script’s insights really end. And while Navarrette is able to elevate the material, it’s the opposite for Michael Johnston, who feels like he’s drowning trying to make even the smallest gesture or line of dialogue work here.

There’s a moment where Johnston’s character asks Nikki, “What would be so wrong with being with me?,” which for maybe the first time felt like a mildly intriguing look into his psyche. It was horrifying to hear after everything he had seen that this was the first question he would think to ask Nikki in this specific moment, and I wanted to scream, “Yes, let’s dig into that!,” but two seconds later we were sitting in a car waiting for the next big obvious jump scare coming around the corner to wow us with how totally fucked up this all is. Give me a break.

I don’t know, I found this whole thing miserably tedious, with its few bright spots only serving to further frustrate things, given where the potential felt like it was possibly there before it succumbed again to its basest desires for empty provocation. The whole tale is woefully predictable, and all it has to fall back on is that shock value which was never exciting. Inde Navarrette very much innocent though, as she delivers one of the best horror performances in recent years. Credit to her for standing out despite everything else going on here.
