Everything about its high-concept cringey teen rom-com turned gory possession movie and sense of style (grey palette, underlit shallow focus symmetry, visceral jump scare sound design) is readymade to slide alongside the Philippou’s or Creggar. You'll be surprised to learn this Curry Baker kid is a YouTube sketch comedian! And on one level that did kind of give this a bit of a ceiling for me, just how obviously it’s chasing its own commercial packaging aspirations.

But on the other, how this goes about stretching such a one-note premise (teen boy secretly pining for cool girl he has a crush on wishes she would fall in love with him and comically grim monkey’s paw antics ensue) to nearly 2 hours and keeps it constantly moving and escalating was pretty impressive. Even before it gets into the gross genre extremity it had a theater crowd groaning in discomfort with how close in proximity to the psychological headspace we are with this insecure, paralyzed "nice guy" making bad courtship decisions that the movie then of course punishes him for when things escalate into supernatural horror. And the level of sheer unpleasant cruelty with which it eventually takes this gruesome co-dependent (and pointedly nonconsensual!) dynamic is admirably frank and nasty, and ruthlessly shifts how you feel about this selfish, cowardly character pretty quickly.

My favorite details were all the unsettling and upsetting glimpses into what it might look and feel like to lose autonomy over your body (the scream on the phone call, the begging for death in sleep bit, the ending duh!), as they were a lot more of an interesting angle to take on this subject matter than the "crazy gf" shock-comedy it often reverts back to. That being said, shoutout to this Inde Navarrette actress who totally knocks those low-hanging uncomfortable laughs out of the park anyway, and whose truly remarkably funny, scary, uncanny and sad performance this is basically a showcase for. Every little stare, smile, disgusting bit of violence or body (and body fluid) horror she does has a manic fixation to it that just keeps getting more and more intense until it's breaking point. And boy does it break! Similarly to Smile or Talk to Me, this is gonna kill on opening weekend with a multiplex crowd.

The rhythm of this thing makes it feel so squirmy and alive. Every nightmarish scare and every dreamy wish is scored by this thrumming, hungry synth score and each of these moments is snapped in two by a hard cut to silence at the most abrupt time. These auditory cuts come consistently throughout the film, yanking us out of the film’s spell again and again. It’s like the film is screaming at us. Snap out of it! Look at what’s become of these people! That poor, poor girl! It’s all kind of absolutely major actually.

Nothing here would be half as good if it weren’t for Inde Navarrette. The scares, the jokes, everything in between hinges on her ability to commit and shoulder almost the full weight of the film. And she does so with ease, like she was born to do it. Her work here is genuinely, truly, deeply terrifying. It’s quite frankly awe-inspiring to take in and reflect back on. Truly a standout performance of the 2020s horror releases.

Obsession is nasty. It’s mean. It’s shockingly cruel. It very clearly revels in making its puppy dog eyed protagonist suffer for his actions as much as possible. It’s a very good film. I think, however, the more you pick at the framing of Obsession, the bloodier the mess you’re left with instead of an intended reprieve. There’s a constant sense of disgust that surrounds Bear for what he’s done, but it’s often at odds too with the natural sort of empathy that can form from watching something so awful exclusively through his perspective. The film can identify the unlikability of what he does but I’m not sure it’s committed to fully leaning into that headspace because the film is specifically built around his experiences. The rare, fleeting moments where Nikki’s experience are put on display are easily the scariest and most haunting here. Ultimately, it’s a gripe I can stomach and push through… but it does leave an aftertaste I can’t quite fully ignore.

Wanted to let this one sit with me before writing anything about it.

Firstly, I think this is a generational example of a performer meeting such a specific character, captured vividly through evocative technique and thoughtfully directed. What a truly sensational way to meet Inde Navarrette. Instantly sits in the pantheon of the greats of horror performances like Lupita Nyong'o in Us or Ruth Gordon in Rosemary's Baby.

The high of watching this bubbling bunny boiler in a packed cinema (all sneaking off to a Tuesday afternoon screening, mind you) is potently undeniable. An enveloping experience that pushes you further on the hook with each development.

Where I've really needed to, or rather wanted to sit with it, is in the key thematic of all horror, really, the narrative push of transgression. It's both obvious and odd here. Effectively obvious because it so clearly plays on the theme of the predatory, controlling nastiness of "nice guys". Where its odd, and perhaps interestingly so... the true transgression arises in an exponentially growing way from Bear's continued behaviour and choices. The transgression is hardly making the wish itself, while it is, of course, entitled and selfish thinking, how is the guy to know it could possibly result in it coming true? The true transgression comes later, and it's far more disturbing, and the punishments are powerful.

And that's where it actually becomes far more interesting. This is a horror film, not just from the perspective of the transgressor but from the villain. When that clicks is when Obsession becomes genuinely special. Think this one is going to stick around awhile, inspiring new generations of horror viewers to interact with film on a more engaged level.

After this, I think I may have been a little unfair towards Backroom, which looks like Citizen Kane compared to Obsession. I’m not sure if terms like “mise-en-scene” and “blocking” actually apply here, not to mention “background.” Indeed it’s the most egregious example I’ve seen yet of the center-framed, extreme shallow focus, elevated solipsism of the nu-horror house style. Inde Navarrette is fine, but with a crew of gen Z actors this far removed from their surroundings (and indeed homogenous space-time), their heads/upper bodies almost begin to float. Their facial expressions seem more influenced by emojis than they are human behavior. Can a film still be called a film when its characters are framed as animatronic bobble-heads who exist in a void of negative space? I’m honestly not sure. I always thought cinema was something based on spatial relations, movement through time. But maybe that was naive idealism on my part. Somehow Obsession exists in a purely psychological, immaterial plane without any outside world. Most of this could have been shot in front of a green screen. I wonder, Where are the films that look outward (to ecology, technology, military etc) to discover horror? I’m tired of this constant whining, me-me-me, toxic abusers blah blah blah. Even psychological horrors about abuse like Possession or Repulsion used to use their subjective POVs as an inroad into feminist critiques while never forgoing the horror of space/domestic environment itself.

Instead, Obsession is very much a part of the recent trajectory of genre film focused on maximizing contrived discomfort or “cringe” in exchange for everything else that might function as an artistic expression of human suffering or social rupture. Similar to how the background of the frame—which was once a rich tapestry of objects and their symbolic relations, frames-within-frames—is reduced to nothing more than a blurred-out smudge, so too is the subtext conflated with surface, leaving only flat one-dimensionality in both form and content. Yeah, it’s a “mean” film, but like most things, meanness is only really mean when juxtaposed with a touch of softness or lightness, made tragic for their out-of-reachness. In short it’s a deeply undialectical film, nothing has any opposition or inverse, peaks and valley all flattened into an insipid brown sludge filter.

As for its content, we have a “be careful what you wish for” Twilight Zone concept stretched 4x past its original runtimes. Much like The Drama, the “what if” speculative scenario is the film’s entire thrust. And while it thankfully skips the trauma-as-metaphor of most nu-horror, this is replaced by something arguably more offensive (while arriving at the same themes of mental illness): the horror of dating a woman with BPD told entirely from the POV of the abuser. I guess it’s supposed to function as a critique, forcing us to see male manipulator soft boi Bear (he makes this face at one point 🥺) as the victim and Nikki as the monster, but the film completely shoots itself in the foot by the end with its unearned overtures towards Eros + Thanatos dark romanticism. Manages to include my two least favorite nu-horror tropes anyway; an innocent person getting their face smashed into a pulp; and a possessed person “trapped in their own body” self-harming by smashing their very own face (this happens twice because the writers don’t know how to structure a scene so as to evoke emotional resonance without building up to a "bit" - this being an extended YouTube sketch - of depraved and cruel shock value. Except by the third face smash, the gimmick has lost even shock, leaving only an embarrassing and nihilistic lack of imagination. If I could erase Hereditary and its effects from collective consciousness I would). Sorry but I’m so serious when I say films like this are the death of the medium, blurring the lines between “films” and “content” (and vice versa) ever more. No more megaplex trips for me, at least for a while.

Elvin Bishop made it sound so sweet with his 1975 hit song, “Fooled Around and Fell in Love”, but it's not. In Curry Barker's OBSESSION (2025), he takes that notion, a wickedly simple idea of a love potion number 9 (the song or the film, you pick), and morphs it into an intimate and perverse experience that features horror's next great performance from Inde Navarrette as Nikki, and anyone who watched CW's Superman & Lois (2021-2024), she's good. Here, she's damn good. A mix of Isabelle Adjani and Mia Goth from their iconic performances. Stuck in the friend zone, that vortex, Baron (Michael Johnston) is debating when is the right time to tell Nikki his feelings that he's been hiding from her. Lacking a little confidence, he happens to half-heartedly buy a “One Wish Willow” from a mystic New Age shop as a joke only to mess with it to appease his incompetence of asking Nikki out. The problem is, the wish works, and Nikki loves him now so, so, so, so, so, so much. The idea came from an unlike source of inspiration: The Simpsons (1989-present). “Bart gets a monkey paw and causes a bunch of chaos,” Barker tells Variety. “I was thinking that I’ve never seen a straight crazy horror where…we’ve seen ‘be careful what you wish for’ tons of times. But we’ve never seen my version of it. I instantly started thinking about what I could do with that.” Barker somewhat exploded on the scene with his ultra-indie MILK & SERIAL (2024 – my review), a micro-budgeted film that he uploaded to YouTube, one because the film is only an hour, and two, for the access of it, something every indie struggles with. It caught the attention of Jason Blum from Blumhouse, who immediately wanted to produce his next film. That would be OBSESSION. “Barker tap[s] into universally relatable emotions, hooking the audience into the central situation before spinning it off in supernaturally chilling directions,” writes Michael Gingold.

It's easy to get behind Baron’s, or as his friends call him, Bear's, wish. Who hasn't been in this situation where you like a girl so much, but timing, or that dreaded friend zone, keeps those emotions at bay. What if a wish, a simple fairy tale wish, could solve that? And it's even easier if that girl is Inde Navarrette. Their chemistry is real and organic, which makes the slow descent into madness and crazy town behavior all that more alarming. It's also claustrophobic; the camera is usually up tight to the actors and the framing is an old box square, and not wide. Barker adds, “I wanted to shoot this center-composed and have extra head space because I wanted it to feel uncomfortable in its loneliness. There’s something about center-composed that forces you to look and pulls you in in a way that traditional composition may not. Ele segue uma tendência cada vez mais recorrente do terror contemporâneo nessa tentativa de fundir a austeridade estética popularizada pela A24 com elementos gráficos e imediatamente sensoriais do terror comercial.

É um movimento que aparece com força em filmes como Sorria, Fale Comigo, Barbarian, e outras obras que tentam equilibrar uma encenação mais “prestigiada” e atmosférica com explosões pontuais de violência.

O filme parece completamente consciente desse modelo industrial e estético, quase como se já nascesse pensando nesse espaço híbrido entre o terror de festival e o terror de multiplex.

A presença da Blumhouse reforça ainda mais essa sensação porque existe claramente um movimento de mercado interessado em absorver certos códigos formais associados à “estética a24” e reaplicá-los dentro de estruturas narrativas mais tradicionais.

Isso está virando até uma espécie de novo padrão do gênero porque mesmo grandes franquias têm incorporado essa lógica, como aconteceu no último Invocação do Mal, em certo grau com Evil Dead Rise, Alien Romulus e provavelmente continuará acontecendo em futuros projetos ligados a propriedades enormes e a cineastas de terror que seguem essa cartilha, como Resident Evil e Massacre da Serra Elétrica.

Mas talvez o aspecto mais singular do filme esteja na maneira como o diretor articula isso com o humor. Não um humor escrachado ou explicitamente cômico, mas um humor de desconforto e quase de humilhação.

Existe algo perversamente engraçado no modo como o protagonista é colocado em situações degradantes e principalmente na maneira imprevisível como a personagem da Inde Navarrette atravessa a narrativa.

As ações dela oscilam o tempo inteiro entre o desespero genuíno, o comportamento irracional e uma espécie de comicidade involuntária extremamente estranha.

E isso funciona porque o filme entende que o exagero pode produzir tensão e entretenimento simultaneamente. Em muitos momentos, as situações são tão extremas e absurdas que acabam funcionando quase numa chave lúdica, mas sem romper totalmente a atmosfera opressiva.

Esteticamente, existe um trabalho muito eficiente com os interiores e com a própria limitação orçamentária da produção. Os espaços fechados criam uma sensação constante de aprisionamento e ajudam a construir uma claustrofobia bastante sufocante.

Ao mesmo tempo, essa economia espacial faz com que a palavra ganhe um peso enorme dentro da encenação.

O filme depende muito de diálogos (alguns relativamente longos), mas eles raramente soam expositivos ou cansativos porque estão organicamente integrados à progressão da tensão.

Existe um cuidado muito grande em transformar conversa em ameaça e hesitação em suspense. Nesse sentido, a atuação se torna bem fundamental para sustentar o ritmo e a Inde Navarrette se mostra como o verdadeiro centro gravitacional de tudo.

Sem a performance dela, provavelmente muita coisa desabaria. Porque a proposta toda do longa depende bastante da permanência emocional da personagem em cena e a atriz consegue sustentar isso através de uma atuação simultaneamente desesperada e melancólica.

Eu gosto bastante do formalismo da decupagem e da precisão visual com que algumas cenas são organizadas, mas também acho que o filme reproduz certos vícios estéticos muito característicos dessa geração pós-A24.

Os enquadramentos em ângulos frontais excessivamente simétricos, a janela mais fechada e quadrada, o controle rígido da composição já começam a adquirir uma aparência meio genérica, quase como uma linguagem padronizada do “terror artístico contemporâneo”.

E embora esses elementos funcionem muito bem para restringir o olhar do espectador e intensificar a sensação claustrofóbica, às vezes a decupagem parece excessivamente travada.

Existem momentos em que a encenação prioriza tanto a manutenção dessa estética calculada que acaba sacrificando possibilidades mais dinâmicas de movimentação e interação entre os corpos.

Algumas cenas claramente pedem uma câmera mais livre, mais instável ou mais agressiva, mas o filme prefere permanecer preso a um rigor visual que, em certos momentos, soa mais como convenção estética imposta do que como necessidade dramática.

OBSESSION is a strong indie horror feature debut from Curry Barker. His ability to clearly establish his premise (“be careful what you wish for,” especially if it’s to be with your crush), utilize effective jump scares, mix horror and comedy, and particularly, his unnerving use of the uncanny valley (at times evoking “Smile”) all proves he is a filmmaker already showing plenty of signs of early promise. Yet the concept feels stretched too thin to fully sustain a feature-length narrative. Still, Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette deliver twistedly fun performances in this rom-com gone horribly, fatally, wrong.

What's great is that there's a lot you can read into the movie, but at the same time none of it really matters. At its core, it's just a blast, taking the very simple ideas of a wish gone wrong and love taken to its logical extremes and just letting things roll. Its bones are old but the flesh is new, taking these time-tested elements and speaking of them in the language of a younger generation versed in a completely different set of neuroses.

It's really funny and horrific that Nikki's strange behavior can be written off as her having some sort of crashout, or her maybe relapsing into drugs. Bear is the avatar of the Internet "nice guy," building his identity around unrequited love, choosing to see himself as noble for quietly pining for a girl. The movie is so good at revealing the rapaciousness of this pretense, Bear barely able to conceal the actual disdain he has for his supposed object of affection.

There's so much good going on. I love how clear it is from the start just how bad a friend Ian really is. And Bear is so self-centered that he doesn't even see it. I love the little drop of Nikki making the distinction between romance and a love story, and Bear saying that it's all the same thing. The story that Nikki reads at the party is a work of genius, and would be the most talked about thing on BookTok for months. I'm not sure I like the bits with Sarah, and I think Ian coming back to the house later was odd, but none of it detracts from just how fun and smart the movie can be.

But really, the most remarkable thing about the movie is Inde Navarette, whose facial expressions are basically the core of the film. She sells it all, finding all sorts of surprising ways to contort her face to express the sheer amount of wrong in the situation. The film uses all sorts of tricks to make Nikki feel like something from outside of reality, but her face really does most of the work.

The film keeps blurring the line between affection and possession. Even the framing and cinematography is infected by that idea. The camera is so fixated on them, trapping them inside the frame. There's this persistent uncertainty where their romantic gesture feels one step away from becoming something deeply unsettling. That's what makes the filmmaking so clever to me. On paper it's a tiny film with a modest budget, but it never feels small. Director understands exactly what to show, what to hide, and when to let your imagination do the rest. The result feels far bigger than its budget has any right to. It pulls off the kind of unnerving, skin-crawling atmosphere that plenty of studio horror films with ten times the money can't even get close to.
